title: Surah, Ayah, Juz': Order, Names and Style
bigQuestion: How is the Qur'an put together, and why does its order and sound matter to the people who read it?

story.title: Three Lines and Forty
story.kicker: Two surahs sit on facing pages. One is over in a breath. The other runs on and on.
paragraphs: Dario opened the borrowed copy near the back, where his teacher said the short chapters live. On the left page, one *surah* took up three lines. Its name at the top said Al-Kawthar, 'Abundance.' He counted the verse markers: three small circles. That was the whole chapter. On the facing page, another surah began and did not stop. He turned the page. It kept going. The heading said it had forty verses.

The copy was in Arabic, but the class had a public-domain English translation open beside it. Pickthall's 1930 version printed the surah names in English, so Dario could match them up. The three-line surah spoke of a gift and a prayer. The long one, Surah 78, An-Naba, 'The Tidings,' opened with a question: what are they asking one another about? Then it listed mountains, sleep, night, day and rain, one after another, like a drumbeat.

His teacher walked past and stopped. 'Notice anything?' she asked. Dario said the short one felt like a song and the long one felt like a speech. She nodded. 'Both come from the Mecca years, Muslims say. The really long ones, near the front, mostly come from Medina. The book is not in the order it was first spoken.' Dario flipped to the front. Surah 2 filled page after page: rules about fasting, debts, marriage, and a story about a cow.

That night Dario tried to explain it to his older brother. 'It is like a playlist,' he said. 'The tracks are not in the order they were recorded. The long ones are first. The short ones with the strongest beat are at the end. And some chapters start with letters that nobody is sure about.' His brother asked what the letters meant. Dario said that was the point. Nobody agrees, and scholars have argued about it for more than a thousand years.
story.think: Dario said the short surah felt like a song and the long one felt like a speech. What might make a chapter feel one way or the other?

lessons.title: One Hundred Fourteen Chapters
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an has 114 surahs, arranged roughly from longest to shortest, and each surah is made of ayahs, or verses.
reading: Open any printed copy of the Qur'an and you will find 114 chapters. Each chapter is called a *surah*. The word is Arabic. Some scholars connect it to a word for a row or a wall of a city, a set-off section. Each surah is divided into short units called ayahs. An *ayah* is a verse, but the word also means a sign, a mark that points to something. The Qur'an uses the same word for the verses on the page and for signs in nature, like rain or the stars.

The surahs are not all the same size. Surah 2, Al-Baqarah (The Cow), is the longest with 286 ayahs. Surah 108, Al-Kawthar (Abundance), is the shortest with 3. Most Muslim scholars count about 6,236 ayahs in the whole book, though older counting systems differ by a few dozen, because they mark verse endings in slightly different places. The count of surahs does not change: 114 in every copy.

Very roughly, the book runs from long surahs to short ones. Surah 2 opens the long stretch. By Surah 90 or so, most chapters fit on one page, and the last ten fit on a page together. This is not a strict rule. Al-Fatiha, the first surah, has only seven ayahs, and a few long surahs sit among shorter ones. But the general slope, long to short, is one of the first things a reader notices.

Every surah except one begins with the *Bismillah*: In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful. Allah is the Arabic word for God, used by Arabic-speaking Christians and Jews as well as Muslims. The exception is Surah 9, At-Tawbah (Repentance), which has no Bismillah at its head. Muslim scholars offer several reasons. One common view is that it continues Surah 8, and another is that its sharp opening did not fit a line about mercy.

words.d: a chapter of the Qur'an; there are 114
a verse of the Qur'an; the Arabic word also means a sign
the line 'In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful' that opens every surah but Surah 9

look.title: Longest and Shortest
look.cite: Verse counts follow the 1924 Cairo edition, the Kufan counting used in most printed copies
look.prompt: Surah 1 is at the front but is tiny. What does that tell you about the 'longest to shortest' pattern?

check.q: What does the Arabic word ayah mean besides 'verse'?
check.why: Ayah means a sign or mark as well as a verse; the Qur'an uses it for both verses and signs in nature.

check.q: Which surah has no Bismillah at its head?
check.why: Surah 9, At-Tawbah, is the one surah that does not open with the Bismillah.

check.q: How many surahs are in every copy of the Qur'an?
check.why: There are 114 surahs. Thirty is the number of juz', and about 6,236 is the ayah count.

lessons.title: How Surahs Got Their Names
lessons.mainIdea: Surah names usually come from a striking word or story inside the chapter, and many surahs have more than one name.
reading: Surah names are not titles the way a novel has a title. Most come from a memorable word or story somewhere in the chapter, often near the start. Surah 2 is called Al-Baqarah, The Cow, because of a story in verses 67 to 73 about the Israelites being told to sacrifice a cow. The cow is not the main subject of the 286 verses. It is simply a name people could remember and say.

Other names work the same way. Surah 16 is An-Nahl, The Bee, from a passage that says God inspired the bee to build its home in the hills and trees (16:68). Surah 29 is Al-Ankabut, The Spider, from a line that compares those who trust in anything besides God to a spider building a flimsy house (29:41). Surah 105 is Al-Fil, The Elephant, from a story about an army with an elephant. Surah 19 is Maryam, named for the mother of Isa (Jesus).

Some surahs have several names. The first surah is Al-Fatiha, The Opening. Muslim tradition also calls it Umm al-Kitab, the Mother of the Book, and the Seven Oft-Repeated. Surah 17 is called both Al-Isra, The Night Journey, and Bani Israil, The Children of Israel. Most Muslim scholars hold that the names came from the Prophet or his companions. In this view the names are not part of the revealed text itself. A few scholars argue for a stronger view.

In a printed copy, the heading of each surah usually gives the name, the number of verses, and whether tradition places it in Mecca or Medina. That heading is a scholar's label, added to help readers, like a table of contents. Knowing this helps a student read the page: the name is a handle, not a summary.

words.d: The Cow, the name of Surah 2, the longest surah, from a story inside it
'the Mother of the Book,' another name Muslim tradition gives Al-Fatiha, Surah 1

look.title: Naming by a Word Inside
look.text: Surah 2, Al-Baqarah, is 286 verses long. It covers fasting, pilgrimage, debts, marriage, the story of Adam, the change of the direction of prayer, and much more. Its name, The Cow, comes from a short story in verses 67 to 73. Imagine naming a whole school year after one field trip that everyone remembered.
look.prompt: Why might a memorable word make a better name than a summary for a chapter that people learn by heart and recite aloud?

check.q: Where does the name of Surah 16, An-Nahl (The Bee), come from?
choices: The surah is entirely about bees
The surah was revealed near a beehive
A passage inside it mentions the bee
It is the sixteenth animal named in the book
check.why: Most surah names come from a striking word inside the chapter; 16:68 speaks of the bee.

check.q: Umm al-Kitab, the Mother of the Book, is another name for which surah?
check.why: Muslim tradition gives Al-Fatiha several names, including Umm al-Kitab and the Seven Oft-Repeated.

check.q: What do most Muslim scholars say about the surah headings in a printed Qur'an?
choices: They are labels added to help readers, not part of the revealed text
They were written by later Christian translators
They are the first verse of each surah
They were added only in the 1924 Cairo edition
check.why: The heading with name, verse count and Meccan or Medinan label is a scholar's aid, like a table of contents.

lessons.title: Parts for Reading: Juz' and Hizb
lessons.mainIdea: Besides surahs, the Qur'an is divided into 30 equal parts (juz') so the whole book can be read in a month, and each juz' into halves and quarters.
reading: Surahs are the Qur'an's own chapters. But readers long ago added a second set of divisions that has nothing to do with subject. The book is cut into 30 nearly equal parts, each called a *juz'* (plural ajza'). A juz' can start or end in the middle of a surah, because the goal is equal length, not meaning. Read one juz' a night and you finish the whole Qur'an in the 30 nights of Ramadan, the month of fasting.

Each juz' is split again into two halves, each called a *hizb*, giving 60 in all. Each hizb is marked at its quarters. A printed copy shows these divisions in the margin with small symbols, so a reader can stop at a quarter, a half, or a whole part and know exactly where to begin again tomorrow. Many Muslims use a hizb as a daily reading portion outside Ramadan.

There is also a division into seven parts, the manazil, for those who want to finish the book in a week. It is less common today. What all these systems share is that they are practical. They answer a reader's question, how much should I read tonight, rather than a scholar's question about themes. The surah and the ayah belong to the text. The juz' and hizb belong to its readers.

During Ramadan nights, many mosques hold a special prayer called tarawih. A reciter moves through one juz' each night. Over the month the congregation hears the whole book. In Chicago, as in cities across the world, some families choose a mosque partly by who leads these nights. The sound of the recitation matters to them.

words.d: one of 30 equal parts of the Qur'an, used for reading it in a month; plural ajza'
half of a juz'; the Qur'an has 60
extra night prayers in Ramadan in which a reciter often reads one juz' a night

look.title: Ways of Dividing the Book
look.cite: Standard divisions marked in most printed copies, including the 1924 Cairo edition
look.prompt: Which of these divisions follow meaning, and which follow length? How can you tell?

check.q: Why can a juz' begin in the middle of a surah?
choices: Because the juz' divides the book by equal length, not by topic
Because each juz' is one surah
Because the surah is too hard to read
check.why: The 30 ajza' are about equal length for reading in a month; they ignore surah boundaries.

check.q: How many hizb are there in the whole Qur'an?
check.why: Each of the 30 juz' has two hizb, so there are 60.

check.q: Which division belongs to the text itself rather than to a reading plan?
check.why: Surahs and ayahs are the Qur'an's own units; juz', hizb and manazil were added by readers for pacing.

lessons.title: Short Surahs, Strong Beats
lessons.mainIdea: Surahs that Muslim tradition places in Mecca tend to be short, rhythmic and urgent, calling people to one God and warning of judgment.
reading: Muslim tradition divides the surahs by where the Prophet Muhammad was living when they were first recited. Mecca was his home from about 610 to 622. Medina was his home from 622 until his death in 632. Printed copies label each surah Meccan or Medinan. About 86 are counted as Meccan and 28 as Medinan. Scholars debate a few, and some surahs mix verses from both periods.

Meccan surahs are usually short. Their lines are brief and end in rhyme or near-rhyme. They speak with urgency about one God, about the signs of God in the sky and earth, about the Last Day when people are judged, and about caring for the poor and the orphan. Surah 81, At-Takwir (The Overthrowing), opens with a chain of images: when the sun is folded up, when the stars fall, when the mountains are set moving.

Read aloud in Arabic, these surahs have a beat. Lines are close in length and their endings ring. Scholars of Arabic style call the effect *saj'*, rhymed prose, and note that Meccan surahs use it most. Muslims say the sound is part of the meaning: a warning should sound like a warning. Historians note that early listeners in Mecca were used to poets and oral speech, so the form spoke to its first audience.

Muslim tradition tells that these years were hard. The early Muslims were a small group in a city that mostly rejected them. Many scholars connect the Meccan surahs' themes, patience, trust in God, judgment coming, to that setting. Reading a surah with its period in mind is one of the first tools students of the Qur'an learn to use.

words.d: a surah Muslim tradition places in the years in Mecca, c. 610 to 622; usually short and rhythmic
rhymed prose; short lines with rhyming endings, common in Meccan surahs
the Day of Judgment, when the Qur'an says every person will be judged; a major Meccan theme

look.title: When the Sun Is Overthrown
look.text: When the sun is overthrown, And when the stars fall, And when the hills are moved,
look.cite: Qur'an 81:1–3, Surah At-Takwir (The Overthrowing), trans. Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: Each line begins with 'when.' What does this repeated pattern do to the listener, and what is the passage building toward?

check.q: About how many surahs does Muslim tradition count as Meccan?
check.why: About 86 surahs are labeled Meccan and 28 Medinan, though a few are debated.

check.q: What is saj'?
choices: rhymed prose with short ringing line endings
a part of the Qur'an read in a week
check.why: Saj' is rhymed prose, the sound pattern common in short Meccan surahs.

check.q: Which theme is most typical of Meccan surahs?
check.why: Meccan surahs stress one God, the signs in nature and the Last Day; laws belong mostly to Medina.

lessons.title: Oaths and the Last Day
lessons.mainIdea: Many Meccan surahs open with oaths sworn by things in nature, a form early Arabic listeners knew, leading into a warning or a promise.
reading: A striking feature of Meccan surahs is the oath. A surah may open by swearing by the morning light, the night, the sun, the fig and the olive, or the galloping horses of a dawn raid. Surah 91, Ash-Shams (The Sun), swears by the sun and its brightness, the moon that follows it, the day that shows it, and the night that covers it. Surah 103, Al-Asr, swears by the passing time.

In Arabic, the oath is an old and serious form. A speaker swears by something to make what follows carry weight. In the Qur'an the oath almost always leads to a claim: that the human soul faces a choice, that people are in loss unless they do right, that the dead will be raised. Muslim commentators such as al-Tabari (d. 923) discuss what each thing sworn by means and why God would swear by a created thing. Several answers are offered.

The Last Day is the topic these oaths most often introduce. The Qur'an describes it with pictures of the world coming apart, the sky splitting, graves opening, and every person seeing what they did. Muslims believe this day will come. The surahs of this kind, such as 99, Az-Zalzalah (The Earthquake), and 101, Al-Qari'ah (The Calamity), are among the shortest and most vivid in the book.

For a student of the text, the oath is a signal. When a surah opens with 'By the...' you can expect a short, intense chapter. It is likely from Mecca and likely about judgment or the human heart. Recognizing the form is like recognizing a sonnet by its fourteen lines. It tells you what kind of thing you are reading before you read it.

words.d: a solemn promise sworn by something; many Meccan surahs open with one, such as 'By the sun'
Surah 103, 'The Declining Day,' three verses opening with an oath by time

look.title: By the Declining Day
look.text: By the declining day, Lo! man is a state of loss, Save those who believe and do good works, and exhort one another to truth and exhort one another to endurance.
look.cite: Qur'an 103:1–3, Surah Al-Asr (The Declining Day), trans. Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: The oath is one line, the claim is one line, and the exception is one line. What is the surah saying keeps a person out of 'loss'?

check.q: What usually follows an opening oath in a Meccan surah?
choices: a claim or warning, often about judgment
check.why: The oath gives weight to what follows, most often a claim about the Last Day or the human soul.

check.q: Surah 91, Ash-Shams, swears by which of these?
choices: the sun, the moon, the day and the night
check.why: Ash-Shams opens with oaths by the sun, the moon, the day and the night; the fig and olive open Surah 95.

check.q: Who was al-Tabari?
choices: the scribe who wrote the first copy
a Muslim commentator on the Qur'an who died in 923
the ruler who ordered the standard copy
check.why: Al-Tabari (d. 923) wrote a major tafsir, or commentary, that discusses the meaning of the oaths.

lessons.title: Medina: Law and Community
lessons.mainIdea: Surahs placed in Medina are longer and speak in a calmer voice about law, family, the new community and its dealings with other peoples.
reading: After the *hijra*, the move from Mecca to Medina in 622, Muslim tradition says the surahs changed. The Muslims were no longer a small rejected group but a growing community with a city to run. The Medinan surahs are mostly long. They talk about fasting, prayer, charity, marriage, divorce, inheritance, debts, contracts and war. They address the believers directly: 'O ye who believe.'

The lines are longer, and the rhyme is looser. Surah 2, Al-Baqarah, is the clearest example: it lays out the fast of Ramadan (2:183–185), the rules for writing down a loan (2:282, the longest single ayah in the book), and the direction of prayer. Surah 4, An-Nisa (The Women), deals with orphans, inheritance shares and marriage. Surah 5, Al-Ma'idah, deals with food, oaths and relations with Jews and Christians.

Medinan surahs also tell of events in the community's life. There is the battle of Badr in 624, the battle of Uhud in 625, and the treaty of Hudaybiyyah in 628. They speak about the Jewish tribes of Medina and about Christians. Sometimes the tone is argument and sometimes respect, as People of the Book. Scholars read these verses with their occasions, the moments tradition says they answered. A verse about a specific dispute reads differently from a general rule.

The two voices are not two books. Muslims read Meccan and Medinan surahs as one Qur'an. But knowing the period helps explain why a surah sounds the way it does. A short, ringing chapter about the Last Day and a long chapter about loans are both there, and the label Meccan or Medinan is one of the first things a careful reader checks.

words.d: a surah Muslim tradition places after the hijra of 622, usually long and concerned with law and community
the move of Muhammad and his followers from Mecca to Medina in 622; the Islamic calendar starts here
the Qur'an's term for Jews and Christians, communities with earlier scriptures

look.title: Two Surahs, Two Voices
look.text: Surah 101, Al-Qari'ah, is 11 short verses. It describes a day when people are like scattered moths and the mountains like carded wool, then speaks of scales that weigh deeds. Surah 2:282 is one verse that runs most of a page. It says to write down a loan, have a scribe write it fairly, and bring two witnesses.
look.prompt: Which surah would tradition label Meccan and which Medinan? Name two clues in each that point to your answer.

check.q: Which subject is typical of Medinan surahs?
choices: oaths by the sun and moon
rules for fasting, loans and inheritance
the folding up of the sky
check.why: Medinan surahs deal with the life of the community: law, family, fasting, contracts and war.

check.q: What happened in 622?
check.why: The hijra, the move to Medina, was in 622; Badr was 624, Uthman's copy c. 650, Cairo 1924.

check.q: Why do scholars read a Medinan verse with its 'occasion'?
choices: to know which juz' it belongs to
because a verse answering a specific event reads differently from a general rule
check.why: The occasions of revelation (asbab al-nuzul) give the setting a verse answered, which shapes how it is read.

lessons.title: A Refrain That Repeats
lessons.mainIdea: Surah 55, Ar-Rahman, repeats one question 31 times, a refrain that shapes the whole surah like a chorus.
reading: Some surahs use repetition on purpose. The clearest case is Surah 55, Ar-Rahman (The Beneficent). It lists gifts: the sun and moon on their courses, the stars and trees, the earth spread out with fruit and grain, the two seas, pearls and coral, ships like mountains. After nearly every pair of verses comes the same question, addressed to two listeners at once: Which is it, of the favors of your Lord, that ye deny?

The line appears 31 times in 78 verses. Read aloud, it works like a *refrain* in a song: the verses change, the chorus returns. Muslim commentators say the 'two' addressed are humans and jinn, unseen beings the Qur'an describes as made of fire. The repeated question makes each gift a challenge. A listener cannot hear the list without being asked, again and again, whether they will call any of it false.

Refrains appear elsewhere too. Surah 77, Al-Mursalat, repeats 'Woe unto the repudiators on that day' ten times. Surah 54, Al-Qamar, repeats a line asking whether anyone will take heed. Scholars of literature compare these to refrains in the Psalms and in oral poetry across many cultures. Muslims often say Ar-Rahman is among the most beautiful surahs to hear, and reciters are known for the way they handle its return line.

The refrain is one answer to a student's question: how can a book meant to be heard hold a listener's attention? Repetition gives the ear something to hold. Muslims have memorized the Qur'an for fourteen centuries, and features like this one, tradition says, are part of what makes that possible.

words.d: a line repeated through a text, like a chorus; Surah 55 repeats one 31 times
Surah 55, 'The Beneficent,' known for its repeated question about the favors of God
unseen beings the Qur'an says were made of fire; addressed with humans in Surah 55

look.title: The Return Line
look.text: Which is it, of the favours of your Lord, that ye deny?
look.cite: Qur'an 55:13, Surah Ar-Rahman (The Beneficent), trans. Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930 (the line recurs 31 times in the surah)
look.prompt: Pick any gift a person enjoys daily. If this question followed it, how would the question change the way you think about the gift?

check.q: How many times does the refrain appear in Surah 55?
check.why: The question 'Which is it, of the favours of your Lord, that ye deny?' appears 31 times in Ar-Rahman.

check.q: According to Muslim commentators, who are the 'two' the refrain addresses?
check.why: Commentators read the dual form as addressing humans and jinn together.

check.q: What is a refrain?
choices: a line repeated through a text like a chorus
a part of the Qur'an read in one night
check.why: A refrain is a repeated line; scholars compare the Qur'an's refrains to those in the Psalms and oral poetry.

lessons.title: Parables and Signs
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an teaches through parables (amthal), short comparisons drawn from everyday life, and by pointing to signs in nature.
reading: The Qur'an often explains an idea with a picture. A good word, it says, is like a good tree, its root firm and its branches reaching to the sky (14:24). Those who trust in anything besides God are like a spider building a house, and the spider's house is the frailest of houses (29:41). Those who spend for show are like a smooth rock with a little soil on it, washed bare by rain (2:264). Each of these is a *parable*, in Arabic a mathal.

The Qur'an says openly that it uses such comparisons. It says God does not shy away from using even a gnat as an example (2:26). Commentators note the pictures come from the life of the first listeners. There are date palms, trade caravans, wells, rain on dry ground, a lamp in a niche. Surah 24:35, the Light Verse, compares God's light to a lamp in a glass. Sufi readers over the centuries have written whole treatises on that one image.

Closely related is the idea of the sign. The same word, ayah, names a verse and a sign in the world. The Qur'an tells its listeners to look: at the camel, how it was created. At the sky, how it was raised. At the mountains and the earth (88:17–20). The difference of human languages and colors is called a sign (30:22). Muslims read nature as pointing beyond itself. Historians of science note that this idea shaped how later Muslim scholars valued studying the natural world.

For a reader, parables and signs are the Qur'an's way of being concrete. An abstract claim about trust is hard to hold. A spider's web in a corner is not. Students can practice by finding a parable, naming the picture, and then stating the idea in their own words.

words.d: a short comparison that teaches an idea; in the Qur'an, a mathal, like the spider's house
Qur'an 24:35, which compares God's light to a lamp in a glass; much discussed by commentators
in the Qur'an, something in nature or history that points to God; the Arabic word is ayah

look.title: The Spider's House
look.text: The Qur'an compares people who take protectors other than God to a spider that builds itself a house. The frailest of all houses, it says, is the spider's house, if only they knew.
look.cite: Qur'an 29:41, Surah Al-Ankabut (The Spider), paraphrased from Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: Name the picture and then state the idea behind it in one plain sentence. What makes the spider a good choice for the point?

check.q: What is a mathal?
choices: a scribe who copied the Qur'an
a parable, a short comparison that teaches
check.why: A mathal is a parable; the Qur'an uses many, such as the good tree and the spider's house.

check.q: Which verse is known as the Light Verse?
check.why: Qur'an 24:35 compares God's light to a lamp in a glass; 2:255 is the Throne Verse.

check.q: According to Surah 30:22, what is one of the signs of God?
choices: the difference of human languages and colors
check.why: Surah 30:22 names the creation of the heavens and earth and the difference of languages and colors as signs.

lessons.title: The Mysterious Letters
lessons.mainIdea: Twenty-nine surahs open with single Arabic letters whose meaning is not known; Muslim scholars have offered many readings and no single answer.
reading: Surah 2 begins with three Arabic letters: Alif, Lam, Mim. They are not a word. They are simply letters, read out by their names. Twenty-nine surahs start this way. Some have one letter, like Surah 50 (Qaf) and Surah 38 (Sad). Some have five, like Surah 19, which opens Kaf Ha Ya Ayn Sad. Fourteen different letters are used in all, exactly half the Arabic alphabet. Scholars call them the *muqatta'at*, the disconnected letters.

What do they mean? The honest answer from Muslim tradition is: God knows. Al-Tabari, in the tenth century, listed the many views he had gathered and did not settle on one. Some said the letters are names of God or of the surah. Some said they stand for words. Some said they are a challenge: the Qur'an is made of these same ordinary letters, so try to make its like. Some said they are a call to attention, like clearing the throat before speaking.

Modern scholars, Muslim and not, have added ideas. Some link the letters to the sound of the opening lines that follow. Some note that in most cases the letters are followed by a mention of the Book or the Qur'an itself, as if the letters introduce the text. None of these has become the settled view. A student who says 'nobody knows for sure' is stating the mainstream position accurately.

The letters matter for reading the page. They are recited exactly as letters, drawn out with their full names. They count as verses in some counting systems and not in others. That is one reason ayah totals differ slightly between old systems. It is also a good example of something students of any scripture meet. Here is a feature of the text that its own tradition treats as an open question.

words.d: the 'disconnected letters' that open 29 surahs, such as Alif Lam Mim; their meaning is debated
the three letters that open Surah 2 and several other surahs

look.title: Alif. Lam. Mim.
look.text: Alif. Lam. Mim. This is the Scripture whereof there is no doubt, a guidance unto those who ward off (evil).
look.cite: Qur'an 2:1–2, Surah Al-Baqarah (The Cow), trans. Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: Pickthall prints the letters with periods and no translation. What choices did he have, and why might he have chosen this one?

check.q: How many surahs open with the mysterious letters?
check.why: Twenty-nine surahs begin with muqatta'at; fourteen different letters are used.

check.q: What did al-Tabari conclude about the letters' meaning?
choices: They are names of the scribes
He listed many views and did not settle on one
check.why: Al-Tabari gathered the views of earlier readers and left the question open; that remains the mainstream position.

check.q: How are the letters recited?
choices: They are read as a single word
Each letter is read by its name, drawn out
check.why: The letters are recited by their names, such as Alif, Lam, Mim, not joined into a word.

lessons.title: Seven Oft-Repeated Verses
lessons.mainIdea: Al-Fatiha, seven short verses, opens the book and is recited in every unit of daily prayer; tradition calls it the Seven Oft-Repeated.
reading: The book opens with a prayer. Surah 1, Al-Fatiha (The Opening), is seven ayahs long. It praises God as Lord of the worlds, the Beneficent and Merciful, Owner of the Day of Judgment. It says: Thee alone we worship, Thee alone we ask for help. It asks to be shown the straight path, the path of those God has favored, not of those who earn anger or go astray. It is the only surah that is entirely addressed by people to God.

Muslim tradition connects this surah with Qur'an 15:87, which speaks of seven of the oft-repeated and the great Qur'an. Most commentators read the seven as Al-Fatiha, and the name stuck. The surah is repeated because it is recited in every rak'ah, every unit, of the five daily prayers. A Muslim who prays the required prayers says it at least seventeen times a day. It is the first surah children learn.

Its place at the front is not because of length. Muslims say it stands first because it is the door to the rest: a request for guidance, followed by 113 surahs that, in the Muslim view, answer it. Surah 2 begins right after with 'This is the Scripture whereof there is no doubt, a guidance,' as if replying. Commentators such as Ibn Kathir (d. 1373) make exactly this connection.

Comparing translations shows how much rests on a few words. Pickthall (1930) opens 'Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds.' Rodwell (1861) has 'Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds!' Sale (1734) wrote 'Praise be to God, the Lord of all creatures.' Each translator chose whether to keep 'Allah' or write 'God,' and how to render the word for worlds. None is the Arabic. All are readings of it.

words.d: Surah 1, 'The Opening,' seven verses recited in every unit of Muslim daily prayer
one unit of Muslim prayer; Al-Fatiha is recited in each one
a traditional name for Al-Fatiha, from Qur'an 15:87

look.title: Three Translators, One Line
look.text: Pickthall, 1930: 'Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds.' Rodwell, 1861: 'Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds!' Sale, 1734: 'Praise be to God, the Lord of all creatures.' All three are public-domain English versions of Qur'an 1:2.
look.prompt: What does each translator gain and lose by writing 'Allah' or 'God,' and 'worlds' or 'all creatures'? Which would you choose for a classroom, and why?

check.q: Why is Al-Fatiha called the Seven Oft-Repeated?
choices: It has seven verses and is recited in every unit of daily prayer
check.why: The name comes from 15:87 and from the surah's seven ayahs recited in each rak'ah.

check.q: What makes Al-Fatiha different from other surahs in who is speaking?
choices: It is entirely addressed by people to God, as a prayer
It is spoken by an angel
It is the only surah in Medina
check.why: Al-Fatiha is a prayer spoken by worshippers to God; most other surahs are addressed to people.

check.q: Which translator wrote 'the Lord of all creatures' in 1734?
check.why: George Sale's 1734 English translation has 'the Lord of all creatures'; Pickthall and Rodwell wrote 'worlds.'

lessons.title: Why Not in Date Order?
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an is not arranged in the order Muslims say it was revealed; tradition holds the surah order was fixed early, and scholars have built separate lists of the order of revelation.
reading: Muslim tradition says the Qur'an was revealed piece by piece over about 23 years, from c. 610 to 632. The Qur'an itself says it was sent down in stages so that it could be recited slowly and settle the heart (17:106, 25:32). But the book is not printed in that order. The first words revealed, by tradition, are 96:1–5, near the end of the book. Surah 2, at the front, is Medinan and late.

Sunni tradition generally holds that the Prophet set the order of the surahs on instruction. The companions then kept that order when they collected the text. Some early scholars allowed that the companions arranged parts of the order. Either way, the arrangement is old and shared. Sunni and Shia copies have the same 114 surahs in the same order. Scholars note that grouping by length was a common way to arrange collections in the ancient world.

Because readers want to know the order of revelation, lists were made. The 1924 Cairo edition prints a traditional chronological number in each surah heading, drawn from early Muslim reports. In 1860 the German scholar Theodor Nöldeke proposed a four-period order using style as a clue: early Meccan, middle Meccan, late Meccan, Medinan. The two lists agree broadly and differ in details, and both are used by scholars today.

Why does this matter? Reading in book order, a student meets law before warning, community before the lone voice in Mecca. Reading in revelation order, the story of the first community unfolds. Muslims mostly read in book order, and memorize in it. Historians often read in the other order. A good student can do both and say why each order shows something the other hides.

words.d: the sequence in which Muslims say the surahs were first recited, different from the book's order
German scholar who in 1860 proposed a four-period order of the surahs based on style

look.title: Book Order Versus Revelation Order
look.cite: Chronological numbers printed in the surah headings of the 1924 Cairo edition; scholars debate individual placements
look.prompt: Surah 2 is first in length but 87th in this list. Surah 110 is near the end of the book and is listed last. What pattern do you see between length and date?

check.q: By Muslim tradition, which verses were revealed first?
check.why: Tradition places the first revelation at 96:1–5, near the end of the book in reading order.

check.q: Over about how many years does Muslim tradition say the Qur'an was revealed?
check.why: Tradition says about 23 years, from c. 610 in Mecca to 632 in Medina.

check.q: What did Theodor Nöldeke propose in 1860?
choices: a new surah order for printing
a four-period order of revelation based on style
check.why: Nöldeke's chronology divides surahs into three Meccan periods and a Medinan one, using style as evidence.

review.q: The Qur'an's 114 chapters are called what?
review.why: A surah is a chapter; an ayah is a verse; juz' and hizb are reading divisions.
Al-Baqarah has 286 ayahs; Al-Kawthar, with 3, is the shortest.

review.q: A juz' is best described as
choices: a chapter named for a story inside it
one of 30 equal parts for reading the book in a month
review.why: The 30 ajza' divide the book by length so it can be finished in the 30 nights of Ramadan.

review.q: Which feature is most typical of Meccan surahs?
choices: short rhythmic lines, oaths and warnings of the Last Day
long verses on inheritance and loans
review.why: Meccan surahs are short and rhymed and stress one God and judgment; law belongs mostly to Medina.

review.q: The refrain 'Which is it, of the favours of your Lord, that ye deny?' comes from which surah?
The Qur'an's comparison of false trust to a spider's house is an example of a
review.why: Qur'an 29:41 is a mathal, a parable that teaches through a picture.

review.q: What is the mainstream Muslim view on the meaning of the letters Alif Lam Mim?
choices: They mean 'In the name of God'
Their meaning is not known for certain; many views have been offered
review.why: Al-Tabari and later scholars list many readings and leave the question open.

review.q: Why is the Qur'an not printed in the order of revelation?
choices: Tradition holds the surah order was fixed early, roughly by length, and separate lists record the revelation order
The order was lost in a fire
Each mosque chooses its own order
review.why: The book order is old and shared by all Muslims; chronological lists such as the Cairo edition's and Nöldeke's are separate tools.
